speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: To attain this national target, we must significantly decarbonise the land transport sector, which accounts for about 15% of emissions.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The electrification of our vehicle population is key to this effort.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The carbon emissions of an electric car are half that of an internal combustion engine (ICE) car and this will improve as more renewable sources enter our energy mix.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Based on current trends, many of these – in fact, a significant proportion – will be electric vehicles, or EVs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This year, more than 10% of new light vehicle registrations were EVs, up from 0.3% in 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The adoption has been broad-based, with half of all EVs registered to condominium and HDB residents.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Today, we have over 3,600 charging points, which is more than double the number two years ago.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And this means that our charging network is going to expand significantly by the middle of this decade.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As we ramp up the EV charging infrastructure, we must also strengthen the governing regulatory framework.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Last year, Parliament amended the Land Transport Authority of Singapore Act, to assign to LTA the statutory function of promoting and regulating the safe use of EVs in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The proposed Electric Vehicles Charging Bill aims to confer LTA with new statutory powers to administer and enforce a comprehensive regulatory regime.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The first is to ensure that EV chargers are safe, and safely used.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Hence, the Bill proposes to regulate the supply, advertisement, installation, registration, maintenance and use of EV chargers, both portable and fixed, including battery charge and swap stations and pantograph chargers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Second, to ensure the reliability of the EV charging network and services through a licensing regime for EV charging operators.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Third, to promote the accessibility of the EV charging network, by mandating a minimum provision of charging points at certain developments and by lowering the resolution threshold for EV charger installation at strata-titled developments.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Earlier this year, MOT and LTA conducted a public consultation exercise on the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: More than 70 members of the public and industry players responded and were, generally, supportive of the provisions that have been proposed.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Industry respondents recognised the need for a licensing regime for EV charging operators, so as to maintain standards, but requested that compliance costs be kept low.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: My Ministry and LTA will work with the industry to ensure this even as we design an effective licensing regime.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Many also supported the proposed charging provision mandate and some even asked for the mandate to be expanded to cover all developments.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: First, on regulating for the safe use of EV chargers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Today, while the Energy Market Authority (EMA) regulates the installation of EV chargers by Licensed Electrical Workers, the activities of others like charger manufacturers, charger suppliers, charger owners and users are not.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Given the potential fire and other safety hazards, the Bill proposes regulation to cover the entire use cycle of EV chargers and to consolidate the regulatory oversight under LTA.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Clause 6 of the Bill specifies that all chargers supplied in Singapore must belong to a homologated model that meets the national charging standard, which is Technical Reference 25, or TR25, and it was revised earlier this year.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Clause 15 of the Bill prohibits the advertisement of non-approved EV charger models, including online or digital advertising.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The Bill empowers LTA to direct the advertiser to stop further publication of the advertisement, disable access to the offending advertisement or publish a corrective advertisement.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As new and emerging charging solutions may not comply with TR25, Part 4 of the Bill allows LTA to administer a special authorisation regime for such chargers to be trialled under controlled conditions, until they are, eventually, incorporated into our main standards.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: To ensure accountability for the proper use and maintenance of EV chargers, clause 22 allows LTA to maintain a national Register of EV chargers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The person in charge and control of an EV charger, which is typically the owner, must register the charger with LTA and will be the registered responsible person required to ensure that it is properly maintained and periodically inspected by a qualified person.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: To ensure safe installation, the Bill and accompanying subsidiary legislation will require chargers to be certified as fit for charging electric vehicles by qualified persons, which includes Licensed Electrical Workers (LEWs) and charging equipment specialists.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The installation of fixed chargers must also be overseen by LEWs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In addition, the Bill also has safeguards against unsafe charging.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: For example, EV chargers capable of charging detachable EV batteries will not be allowed in residences because of the risk of battery fires.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Also, a manufacturer or supplier who knows of a safety defect in the charger or charger model it has supplied must inform persons with charge and control of such chargers on how to rectify the defect and, subsequently, report to LTA upon the completion of rectification work.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The services provided by such EV charging operators will include hiring of fixed EV chargers, EV battery swapping and renting of portable EV chargers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Licensing conditions will include the purchase of public liability insurance and correcting EV charging service downtime issues within a specified duration.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: For a start, the licensing regime will only cover EV charging operators that provide charging services to the public, given the focus on commercial EV charging operators.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This coverage can be expanded in accordance with future needs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The Bill also allows for step-in arrangements in respect of a designated licensee.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Under clause 56, the Minister may, by order in the Gazette, prescribe a licensee that is authorised to provide EV charging services as a designated licensee.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: For example, this may be a licensee with a large scale of operations in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: If the licence of a designated licensee is revoked or surrendered, the Minister for Transport may, on the advice of LTA, invoke clause 57 of the Bill to authorise a step-in operator to take over the designated licensee's operations temporarily, for no more than 12 months.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This will minimise disruption and facilitate a smoother transition for the affected EV users.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The intent is for these provisions to be invoked where no short-term commercial arrangement or remedies are available and it will be used as a last resort.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The third objective of this Bill is to promote the accessibility of the EV charging network.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: With more vehicles going electric, all carparks in Singapore will need to provide for EV charging.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Therefore, Part 8 of the Bill mandates the provision of EV charging infrastructure by developers of specified building works and development owners who carry out certain types of electrical works.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: These are, typically, new developments or those undergoing substantial renovation.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The mandate, which will be prescribed in subsidiary legislation, consists of two parts.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: To illustrate, a development that is in compliance will be able to support 7.4 kilowatt (kW) charging points with smart charging capability at about one in five lots.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And in terms of the actual installation of chargers, the developer can comply with the mandate by fitting out about one in 25 lots with such 7.4 kW charging points.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: I am sure everyone understood that technical point.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: But if I may put it in simple terms, what it means is that one part of the requirement is for the electricity capacity that is to be provided and the technical people have used a specific metric applied to the number of parking lots to establish that cap.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The second part of that mandate is on the number of lots.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, while you can have up to one in five of the lots with these chargers, the mandate is really, if you go by slow charging rates, it will amount to about one in 25.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, it is about 4% or 5% of the lots.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: But the mandate is designed to provide the flexibility to deploy a mix of charging points with different power ratings at more or fewer lots, depending on the needs of users.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: For instance, some developers may opt to have more charging lots installed with lower-powered chargers, while others may have fewer lots installed with higher-powered chargers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, there is a trade-off because, for a given electrical capacity, if you choose to have more high-powered chargers, then you have fewer charging stations and vice versa.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Over the past two years, we have received feedback on the challenges faced by strata-titled developments like condominiums in installing EV charging points.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Proposals to install EV charging points may be defeated despite having the majority support of subsidiary proprietors.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Such a proposal must not draw down on the funds of the Management Corporation, and the relevant lease or licence between the Management Corporation and the EV charging operator that enables such a proposal must not last for more than 10 years.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, there is a safeguard around the draw of funds and there is also a safeguard around the duration of the contract.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This Electric Vehicles Charging Bill is an important foundation and first step.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: It is a milestone in Singapore's quest for a sustainable land transport system and in our journey towards net-zero emissions by 2050.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And I commend it to all Members to give it their full support.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is already a lower percentage than the US, UK and the global figure, but it is still a significant piece as we look to cut our carbon emissions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Introducing this framework to regulate safe and efficient charging of EVs is a significant starting step, but it should not be the end.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My speech will not only focus on clarifying how certain provisions in this Bill are going to operate, but also discuss the broader implications on our strategy to transition Singapore's vehicle population from ICE to EVs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, I support Part 8 of the Bill which requires developers undertaking certain building or electrical works to install infrastructure to support the supply of minimum electrical charging capacity, as the Minister has shared earlier.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This helps to future-proof developments that are presently being constructed even as the national EV strategy is being considered and refined.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is, generally, more cost-effective to plan and incorporate such infrastructural elements at the outset, than to require costly variation works midway through the construction works.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, when is Part 8 going to come into force?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would present developments that have already obtained preliminary design and construction approvals be required to modify their plans?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Another question I have is, what is the minimum stage that the planning and construction work has to reach before the Minister would consider exempting a development from the new requirements introduced by Part 8?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Further, is there a particular reason why the new Part 8 requirements will not apply to works carried out by the Government or any public authority on land that they own?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Given the nationwide push for a greener transport infrastructure, I would have thought that the Government would join the effort and take the lead in equipping its developments with the necessary electrical infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, a large part of the Bill serves to regulate the devices that are intended for charging EVs in Singapore, the operators of charging stations and the providers of charging services for EVs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As we are contemplating widespread use of EVs and EV chargers, it is key that we have a regulatory framework to ensure the safety and efficient deployment of EV chargers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: From my reading of the Bill, I understand there to be three levels of regulatory control.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Is each of the three levels of control necessary, or is it regulatory overkill?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must be cognisant that each level increases the amount of compliance costs for EV Charging Operators (EVCOs), which could have the effect of increased EV charging costs for end users and even the effect of squeezing out potentially competitive EVCOs from the relatively small market we have in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the longer term, this is all going to have a material impact on the cost of EV charging, which I feel will make or break our efforts to get Singaporeans on board with our vision to transit to EVs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While EV and charger companies can do their part to manage costs, the full package of Government policies, taxes and fees, ultimately, have a major impact on the lifetime cost competitiveness of EV versus ICE vehicles.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It will be useful to have a sense of the extent of the fair value EV charging costs in the future at this juncture.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In relation to the first level of control, LTA will only approve an EV charger model if it is satisfied that the model meets the safety and performance standards prescribed by the regulations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The question I have is: have these regulations been prepared and are they ready to be put into effect immediately?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What are all these safety and performance standards that will be built into the legislation?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is also contemplated that LTA-approved models of EV chargers will be identified with an approved label that is affixed to each EV charger which is intended to be supplied, installed, certified or charged in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What is the applicable fee that would be prescribed for the issuance of an approved label?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Further, what is the applicable fee for the issuance of an additional label where LTA approves a proposed alteration or modification to the EV charger model?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Another question is: is the approved label really the most suitable enforcement mechanism?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Not only are physical labels susceptible to wear and tear which may cause them to peel off the EV charger; more importantly, who is the intended audience of the label?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For the regulator, the presence or absence of a label is unnecessary for it to identify whether an EV charger is an approved model.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For an end-user, I am doubtful that the absence of a label would cause them to avoid using a particular EV charging station.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The second level of control is for LTA to register an EV charger if the EV charger is lawfully certified as fit for charging any EV in Singapore and lawfully installed in accordance with clause 24 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Given that a certifier is obliged to check that an EV charger satisfies the applicable safety and performance standards here, does it not render the first approval-label stage superfluous?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Why is it necessary to separate the approval of EV model and registration of EV chargers into two stages?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We now know from LTA's announcement that these refer to charger equipment specialists and a Licensed Electrical Worker, or LEW, respectively.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are there any plans by the Ministry or LTA to train and recruit more Singaporeans to be LEWs and charger equipment specialists?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are there any targeted numbers of such specialists to support our EV charging push?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While there may already be ITE and Polytechnic courses and programmes in this regard, can we aim to do more, for example, by designing career conversion programmes or Career Transition Programmes around these aims to meet our requirements?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Given the overarching theme of sustainability in relation to this Bill, my humble suggestion is that such records can be uploaded and kept in a centralised electronic repository rather than in paper form.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This will be in line with our general push to digitalise our systems and records.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This would also assist LTA in transposing the necessary information to the register of registered-for-charging EV chargers that it is required to maintain.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I also have a couple of questions on the register to be maintained by LTA.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, what are the concerns that drive the confidentiality provision at clause 22(4) of the Bill?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I note from the public consultation feedback that the key concern is over undue disclosure of commercially sensitive data by the EV charger companies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What commercially sensitive information is LTA register expected to contain?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How would a manufacturer or supplier go about obtaining such confidential information?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As a preliminary question, what is the expected duration for which licences will be valid?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will the conditions of renewal be spelt out clearly in subsidiary legislation?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I ask these questions because I expect an EVCO to have to invest significant capital expenditure at the outset which can only be recouped by its provision of services over time.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It would be important for them to have enough certainty over their projected revenue stream in the mid to long term so as to perform their internal financial calculations for their business.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Also, considering our targets for our EV population and the number of EV charging points, as mentioned by the Minister earlier, does the Ministry have a rough idea of how many licensees it intends to allow to operate in the geographically limited market here?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I recognise that there are potentially a number of operational issues that LTA will need to formulate in consultation with the industry, such as what the optimal licence conditions ought to be.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Considering the importance of this area in the next 10 to 20 years as we work to phase out petrol and diesel vehicles by 2040, there may be value in encouraging a professional body to bring the relevant stakeholders and actors together.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I believe the licensing regime introduced under the Insolvency, Restructuring and Dissolution Act 2018 was implemented quite smoothly, in part because there already existed professional bodies like the Insolvency Practitioners Association of Singapore (IPAS) that was anchoring the professional development and standards in that space.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Third, Part 4 of the Bill specially empowers the Government to make rules to trial non-approved or non-registered EV chargers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I assume they will automatically apply to the existing regulatory sandboxes that are taking place.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On that note, may I ask if there are any interim findings from the ongoing regulatory sandboxes for battery swapping for electric motorcycles?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I had previously raised a Parliamentary Question on this back in October and earlier as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I note that the Bill is technically broad enough to cover battery swapping services.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can I confirm that notwithstanding the Ministry's position that the charging of detachable batteries at home remains disallowed, it is prepared to proceed to register and license battery charge and swap stations, or BCSS, while the regulatory sandboxes are ongoing?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Fourth, can I check if LTA intends to take a proactive and pre-emptive enforcement stance, instead of prosecuting persons only after a particular safety or other incident has occurred?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How does LTA intend to do so beyond mandating periodic inspections of registered EV chargers, which will not flush out cases of unauthorised supply or modification of EV chargers?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Also, what are the enforcement capabilities and resources needed by LTA in the future and if it will meet the rise in enforcement needs?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Given that the road tax for an EV is significantly higher, how the EV charging costs compare with the cost of petrol will be key in determining consumer take-up.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some assurances or controls over future increases in EV charging costs will give some consumers the confidence to take the leap of faith and go with the relatively new EV option.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: HDB and JTC are likely to be the largest landlords with which EVCOs will contract with in Singapore and such tenders are usually conducted by LTA.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: MOT and LTA will have to dynamically continue to manage the relative calibration of all the components to meet Singapore's overall goals and ensure safety at the same time.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Notwithstanding the clarifications sought, I support the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The fundamental problem it seeks to address is this: how LTA and EMA will work together to ensure that the charging infrastructure is sufficient during the transition and, relatedly, how such charging costs will be regulated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I support the Bill but have additional suggestions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The bulk of my speech will address the hard infrastructure issues that are the primary concern of the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, I will conclude with thoughts on how soft infrastructure, in particular our Certificate of Entitlement (COE) system, can also play a role in helping Singapore usher in the electrification of its vehicle fleet.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Throughout, my focus will be on practical considerations associated with this transition process.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Providers are also required to obtain fixed-duration licences and to meet conditions, such as minimal up times and securing public liability insurance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: On the whole, these are in line with best practice international frameworks, such as the UN Global Technical Regulation on Electric Vehicle Safety, albeit it remains somewhat less ambitious than stricter standards, such as the EU Regulation Number 540/2014.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of paramount concern is whether new EV charging stations will adequately address consumer safety concerns, including the risk of electric shocks, battery-related fire and cyber-hacking.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Fires are a particularly salient concern, given a number of recent reports of HDB fires due to Personal Mobility Devices (PMDs) and the general density of our multi-storey parking structures – Minister Iswaran alluded to this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In Sengkang alone, I am aware of at least two over the past two years, and Minister Shanmugam has shared with this House, that there were 18 PMD fires across the island last year, all of which the SCDF and LTA had determined to be due to non-compliance with safety standards.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Beyond fires per se, our humid tropical environment may present greater maintenance challenges which, in turn, calls for more attention to ongoing regulation of the charging infrastructure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What safety features and public education efforts has the Ministry put in place to address such concerns?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: At the moment, the Bill, in Parts 5, 6 and 10, focuses mainly on technical and/or intended offences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The pertinent question is how inadvertent violations that compromise safety can best be handled, as this also tends to be the case with PMD-charging-related fires.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is a good start and has been adopted in other crowded Asian cities, such as Tokyo.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The practical challenge here is how to ensure there are sufficient stations for EV owners wishing to charge their vehicles and, relatedly, how to prevent hogging of said chargers after charging is complete.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, many would enjoy the convenience of being able to charge overnight, which is especially attractive given, at least for now, the lower cost of electricity after hours.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The flip side of the strategy, however, is that it would, typically, preclude the timely relinquishment of the station.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One management approach is to adopt the strategy employed by Tesla which charges a per minute idle fee for vehicles that are already fully charged, with a higher penalty rate if all chargers are also simultaneously fully occupied.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even with such a system, there may be insufficient charging for certain user-type, the so-called "power users", which would be, for instance, taxi cabs and private hire car (PHC) drivers which are likely to be able to charge only during off-peak hours and require longer charging durations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Some degree of calibration would, undoubtedly, be necessary, but one interim step may be for LTA to coordinate with PHC and taxi cab companies to obtain the distribution of their registered drivers and adapt initial installation at multi-storey carparks (MSCPs) accordingly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This could mean pursuing an active policy target that seeks the minimum number of charging points per building as stipulated by law.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Part 13 of the Bill, in particular, clause 97, is designed to expand the network for the Management Corporation Strata Title (MCST) car parks which do not directly fall under LTA and, hence, require more targeted incentive structures to encourage adoption.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is a clear improvement as, previously, some MCSTs may have required as much as 90% vote share to pass the necessary resolution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My Workers' Party colleague Dennis Tan will suggest a tailored approach to the expansion of coverage, especially for industrial premises.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In principle, MCSTs, such as condominiums as well as commercial and industrial developments, should have a strong incentive for charger installation, given the typically higher income profile of residents' overall heightened environmental consciousness of wealthy households, the ongoing flow of tenants and customers for such projects and the likelihood of a profitable income stream.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The ECCG co-funding model should have provided the rest of the necessary boost.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet, the barrier to more widespread adoption seems more psychological than monetary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, inertia is a powerful force and those of us who have lived in condos and served on condo boards understand how apathetic most condo dwellers are about attending the annual general meeting (AGM).

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This leads one to wonder whether more can be done to empower MCST and commercial facilities to roll out even more charging stations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Could policy target higher minimum ratio for stations in non-landed private residences beyond legislation?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This would ensure that these developments do not inadvertently fall behind even while the HDB rollout accelerates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Singapore already has a built-in system for effecting a controlled phase-out of the existing internal combustion engine fleet.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We can do this in at least two ways.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If we were to do so, this would effectively phase out the approximately one-million-strong ICE fleet over the course of the following decade, give or take several tens of thousands of heavy goods vehicles that may be less amenable to electrification.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Then this way we can embark on the EV transition immediately.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And as private charging providers receive even stronger incentives for switching now, they will also step up efforts to expand their networks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This solves, in some part, the chicken and egg problem of EV charger installers waiting for greater EV adoption before increasing charging capacity while potential EV purchasers hold off while they await more charging stations to appear.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The COE system offers additional tools for us to encourage the switch to an EV fleet.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For instance, there is some evidence that drivers of PHCs have expressed reluctance to switch to EVs owing to range anxiety and the much higher operating costs for EVs, estimated at as much as 82% or greater.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet, since PHCs are utilised at about seven times the rate of the average car, they account for a disproportionate share of emissions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One way to compel such switches is to designate a special COE category for PHCs that are also EVs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This riffs off a query that my Sengkang colleague, Louis Chua, had put forward, albeit in the context of concerns over whether PHCs were bidding up COE prices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To the extent that this eventually does raise the cost of regular ICE COEs, we can content ourselves that, at the very least, there is a beneficiary, which is, the environment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Other approaches would be to provide subsidies or to offer a discount off the price of COEs in the PHC-EV category.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Speaker, may I just seek a clarification from the Member?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Did he say that PHC drivers expressed concern about the higher operating cost of EVs?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This is not my own numbers but based on —

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Before I proceed, I would like to declare my interest as the President of Strides Mobility Services of SMRT which has business units that rent out EVs and provides EV chargers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I had previously spoken during the Committee of Supply (COS) debate about how it is important to have enough or sufficient charging stations in HDB estates, private estates and commercial buildings.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This is in order for the EVs to take off.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I am glad to note that the EV Charging Bill has considered some of my recommendations.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This is a strategic and timely move by MOT and LTA.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: To realise our vision, we will need to consider ways to achieve fairness, better affordability and confidence for our EV users.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The lifecycle cost of owning an EV, as compared to owning an ICE vehicle, is much higher.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In other words, owning EVs over the lifespan is higher than owning ICE vehicles in Singapore currently.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Will the majority of car buyers in Singapore buy EVs just because they are pro-environment or think that EVs are greener?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This may not be so, as consumers are very practical and financially savvy.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Even the green-conscious residents in the Nordic countries are also behaving similarly as being cost-conscious.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Norway, currently, has the highest rate of EV ownership in the world, with the most number of EV owners in Norway, compared to other countries.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: EV drivers in Norway get to use toll roads for free, enjoy free parking and are exempted from Norway's high purchase taxes.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We may not take the same route, but some incentives do help to promote EVs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Currently, the EV buyers in Singapore enjoy some tax rebates and incentives.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Would we need to do more, to give this a stronger push?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: When LTA signals its intention to install EV chargers in all HDB car parks, mass market EV adoption is key to the frequent utilisation of the chargers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: To encourage mass market adoption, I also want to suggest that we perhaps give a discount for Category A (Cat A) COE prices for those EV buyers and I suggest that this can be part of the early adopter scheme.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Do I only suggest to have 10% discount on Cat A COE?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Because the Cat A COEs are catered to buyers who are more cost-conscious and it is more likely the Cat A COE cars ply the roads longer than other categories.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: So, by converting them to EVs, we can have a greater impact in reducing carbon dioxide emission.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But we have got to be careful about this.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Instead of creating a separate EV category, as what is suggested by Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, because those who are able to pay for the higher value of EVs, we should not subsidise them.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: And although this eye-catching COE discount early EV adopter scheme can be removed once a critical mass of EVs is on the road or when the prices of EVs have fallen significantly as predicted by industry experts, that would happen in a couple of years’ time.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I would also like to clarify with Assoc Prof Jamus Lim – he said the report said that operating a PHC or taxi equivalent, the cost is 82% higher.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I really doubt this is so because in my experience of renting out EVs, the cost of owning and operating EVs is cheaper as compared to a hybrid or diesel vehicle because of the high mileage incurred by the PHC or taxi.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: At the same time, it is important to cultivate a good EV charging culture to deter hogging of charging points when an EV is fully charged.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But we also do not want to go to the extent where you also charge an idling fee when the EV is fully charged at 4.00 am in the morning.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: There is a balance of how we want to use the idling charge to encourage good behaviour of charging.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Meanwhile, I understand from some industry players that there are teething issues relating to the installation and use of EV chargers in the HDB car parks which I hope Government agencies can help to resolve.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This will lead to a faster transition of ICE vehicles into an EV fleet across our car population.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Instead, HDB – they replied in The Straits Times Forum page – will assess and grant approval on a case-by-case basis to allow EVs, especially commercial EVs, to park at multi-storey car parks, I hope that LTA and HDB can do a systemic review to facilitate parking of electric commercial vehicles at HDB car parks, which will eventually have EV charging facilities.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This will better optimise the use of electric chargers by a range of vehicles and not just private EVs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Thirdly, we understand that the roll-out of EV chargers at HDB car parks is a gradual process.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Currently, only about 200 HDB car parks are installed with EV chargers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Some EV users staying at the precincts beside the existing car parks with EV chargers have to pay parking fees while they charge their EVs overnight.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Thus, I hope LTA can work with HDB to consider making an arrangement to allow EV users staying adjacent to the car parks with EV chargers to park for free while charging their EVs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But it would be good if the agencies can assist until all HDB car parks are installed with EV charges.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I urge LTA to closely monitor the charging fees over time to ensure fairness and affordability.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: At the same time, we would like to avoid the situation where, as what the Minister has said, EV users have to pay a higher charging fee should any of the charging operators exit the market.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: To install EV chargers, only licensed electric workers or LEWs can do so.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: However, many of the LEWs are already engaged in other jobs due to the opening up of our economy in tandem with the easing of COVID-19 pandemic restriction measures.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Moreover, we also need LEWs to maintain the 60,000 EV chargers in time to come.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Thus, I would like to ask the Minister, as what the Chairman of the Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) has said, whether LTA would work with the industry to generate more trained LEWs to sustain the momentum of installing EV chargers in large numbers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In particular, will MOT and LTA be working with Polytechnics and Institutes of Technical Education to train more Singaporeans to be LEWs?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: At the same time, there are also growing concerns of EVs catching fire.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In the last two years, I also had two fire incidents at HDB flats in my Nanyang constituency that involved battery charging of electric personal mobility devices.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: There were casualties from these two incidents, including one death, unfortunately.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Likewise, the safety of EVs cannot be overlooked.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: That translates to seven EV fires a day.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: At the same time, there are also reports indicating that EVs are safer than ICE vehicles.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Hence, I would like to ask the Minister on key lessons which MOT and LTA have gleaned on the safety of EV and EV charging.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We are in the midst of going through an exciting transformation in the transport sector as part of our quest towards the Singapore Green Plan 2030.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The Electric Vehicles Charging Bill has the potential to turbo-charge our transition from the ICE age to the new EV era.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But we cannot overlook the transition issues that have been highlighted above and I hope the Minister can address them.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We recognise that the best way to travel around Singapore is by train or by MRT.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Please take the train as often as possible.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But if you need to drive, consider an EV.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Before I end, I would like to ask Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, who was suggesting that after some years, we will not allow the registration of any non-EV vehicles.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The first has to do with that report.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It has now been raised both by the Member as well as Minister S Iswaran.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The quote was originally by the Grab Group's Vice President for Marketing and Sustainability, Cheryl Goh.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: She had made this statement in a conference and it was reported not just in my original source but also in The Straits Times.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: That is my estimation of the Government's target.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Feted as a breakthrough model, the Leaf was considered one of the most efficient and user-friendly electric cars.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A decade later, Singapore is beginning its journey towards electrification.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In March this year, I spoke briefly on the need for greater electrification of our commercial goods fleet and expansion of charging infrastructure for such a fleet during the Committee of Supply debates.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Minister acknowledged that there are fewer viable cleaner-energy solutions currently available for heavier goods vehicles.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am concerned that such goods vehicles may continue to be a significant contributor to our land transport emissions as a result.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: There is an important point to make here.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Since the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic, e-commerce and the accompanying last-mile deliveries have seen a surge in demand.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The World Economic Forum estimated that last-mile deliveries saw an increase of 25%, with up to 20% of the growth remaining post-pandemic.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As I alluded to in March, with pre-pandemic growth in last-mile delivery increasing carbon emissions by 30% by 2030, a lack of supporting infrastructure to encourage EV adoption could have deleterious effects on our ability to reduce our emissions and meet our carbon-neutral goals as a country.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We should bear in mind that we have a large number of commercial goods and heavy vehicles locally as well as a large number of goods vehicles which come in from Malaysia on a daily basis.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: To that end, while the Ministry has focused on using the "sticks" of the Commercial Vehicle Emissions Schemes (CVES) and the Early Turnover Scheme (ETS) to encourage the adoption of cleaner energy light goods vehicles locally, I would reiterate that a lack of widely available charging infrastructure, particularly for the "brown" goods delivery fleets, is a significant roadblock to our green goals.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Electric Vehicles Charging (EVC) Bill is, certainly, a welcome step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: With to-be stipulated requirements for charging points in buildings, this ensures that the charging infrastructure is established to match the mandated increase in demand.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As the number of charging points required is correlated with the purpose of the building, I urge the Minister to take a tailored approach to each building.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A distribution hub which uses purely EVs may be more likely to require more charging points, compared to a residential block.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As I previously highlighted, an important measure in the deployment of these chargers is the siting and the number of chargers, with a critical mass needed to support charging and minimise queues for charging points.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The EV Charging Bill has taken a step down this path, with a formula-based approach to determining the number of chargers required per building.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Moving forward we should expect the numbers to increase exponentially.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I wonder whether the Minister can share more details as to how the Ministry arrived at the formula that is being used to determine the number of chargers which would be optimum for each car park.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If I assume that an average privately owned EV travels approximately 60 kilometres per hour each day and has a range of approximately 300 kilometres, then the average driver would need to charge his vehicle to full every four days.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This could mean that a significant scaling up of charging points would be necessary, given the current trends.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Is the Minister able to share with the House how LTA expects to keep up with a possible rising demand?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And may I also ask whether LTA is considering building charging points on a larger scale in advance of demand, perhaps even taking on the risk that there might be, in the short term, a little excess and underused capacity?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: My concern is that it will be harder to persuade more to convert to electric cars if they see that the charging facilities are insufficient.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is not even considering that the price of many EVs remain relatively expensive.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: There is also the possible issue that if more people convert to EVs and the EV car numbers were to go up ahead of the building of sufficient infrastructure, there may be a period of frustration for vehicle owners as they cope with insufficient facilities in their immediate vicinity.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Still on EV charging for residential and public car parks, I have received feedback that there are owners who have parked their EVs at parking lots with EV chargers without actually charging their cars.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, I would like to seek an update from the Minister on the progress of our condominiums, office and commercial buildings and other MCSTs on their adoption of EV chargers in their carparks as their timely participation is also important in our country's EV conversion journey.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I now move on to the topic of commercial and industrial usage of EVs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I note that we are already on the Combined Charging System (CCS) charging format; several heavy goods vehicle offerings available globally are already built for this charging format.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The largest of these vehicles are able to tow up to a Gross Combined Weight Rating (GCWR) of 40,000 kilogrammes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is roughly equivalent to a single 40-foot International Organization for Standardization (ISO) container.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This may help to not only enhance the development and use of better technology in our own electrification efforts locally, but it will also help Singapore in our journey towards a low emission future.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It may lead to new technologies which could be exported, giving a boost to the Singapore economy and creating new areas of growth in our manufacturing industry.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As this is a very new sector still developing and evolving, the number of operators is limited, especially for a small market like ours.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My concern is how to ensure that users and consumers can benefit from competitive pricing and, of course, affordability.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My next question, following up on my first point, is how would the Ministry ensure a level playing field for all vendors to compete effectively, for the good of EV owners and drivers?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I think it is important that we have a range of vendors.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Over time, the smaller suppliers may get muscled out of the market, leaving drivers with fewer choices, at which point, they would be at the mercy of the remaining operators.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that the Ministry would implement measures to foster a healthy suppliers' market.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Another point of concern is how do we regulate platform providers to ensure that all imported portable chargers are compliant with the regulations?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Minister share how enforcement will be carried out?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While we have the legislation, how do we enforce effectively while it is still at this early stage to address fire safety concerns?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This trend has, most certainly, boded well for our national EV objectives.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Users are more confident in purchasing an EV, due to availability of EV models, charging infrastructure, competitive costs and access to associated amenities.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: I want to congratulate and thank MOT for the work well done thus far in our EV transition.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The continued deployment of EV infrastructure over the next 10 years is critical in maintaining our pace.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As such, it is timely for MOT to introduce the Electric Vehicle Charging Bill to ensure reliable EV charging services and infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Like elevators in our buildings, EV chargers should meet high standards, with timely maintenance to ensure safe operations.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Given the nascent EV charging technology, I would like to ask the Minister how MOT will establish and review the certification and testing standards.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: How will these new standards affect current owners of EV chargers?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In the future, when these standards evolve, how will it affect EV chargers that were already implemented?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: To ensure a robust EV charging industry, operators will play a significant role in ensuring that EV charging experience is safe and reliable.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As the capital expenditure (capex) investment for an EV charger is substantial, licensing and establishing commercial guidelines are essential to ensure commercial viability, price stability and user reliability.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Also, how long will the licence be valid?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The network and accessibility of the chargers are essential.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As a significant proportion of the chargers will be located on private premises, how will the usage of these chargers be regulated?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Will there be a distinction between EV chargers solely for private and public use?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Can private owners provide charging services on an ad hoc basis?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Another example is: if the chargers are located within a private estate or home, can the public pay for and use the charging infrastructure when visiting these private properties?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: How will this affect chargers on Government premises and Government-linked premises, such as JTC managed properties?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Will these EV chargers be reserved only for staff in the building?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: If there is restricted use clause, will a vehicle that requires emergency charging be able to use these facilities?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The transition phase for any implementation will be dynamic.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: There will be disruption and I am encouraged that MOT and LTA have mentioned that they will work closely with the industry to facilitate the transition.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Bill is set up to make EVs charging safe, reliable and accessible, in hopes of realising the rapid proliferation of EVs and a cleaner, more sustainable Singapore.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The dynamics of car ownership in Singapore, however, are varied and, indeed, ever-changing.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have people who drive every day, people who drive only during the weekends, people who drive to bring their family around, people who drive because of work and people who drive because driving is their work.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And, indeed, I would argue that these varying dynamics need to be taken into consideration, as we single-mindedly eye the prize of a clean sustainable Singapore with the proliferation of EVs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While the total number of new car registrations dipped in the first half of the year, the number of cars registered for private hire was steadily on the rise.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This means that an increasing proportion of cars on the road today are cars that are part of our public transport network, such as our registered for-private-hire vehicles and our over 14,000-strong taxi fleet.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We do have some good tailwinds, however, on the matter though, and, through conversations with our leaders and members at the National Taxi Association and the National Private Hire Vehicles Association, I can feel a good buzzing energy about the move towards EV.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, there are some concerns on the ground.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For those among us who drive cars, we are familiar with the anxieties associated with a near-empty tank and an unknown distance to the next petrol station.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While our seasoned taxi and private hire drivers are familiar with the rhythms of their workhorses and are able to "agar-agar" their refuelling schedules, they seek assurances that anxieties around an empty tank, or battery for that matter, can be dispelled.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The ubiquity of charging stations is not enough; their prominence, locatability and predictability of availability are of utmost importance.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Simply put, taxi and private hire drivers must be able to easily find and get to charging stations and not be caught by their unavailability, for instance, by a long queue of drivers waiting for the charging point to be freed up, even if the driver had come up with the best of journey planning.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Indeed, our drivers may even be charging multiple times a day, throughout the day, especially if the vehicle is fully utilised round the clock, shared by the main hirer and his relief drivers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On concentration, taxi and private hire jobs during peak hours are, predictably, focused on a few major travelling nodes in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This means that charging station availability is challenged, hindering the usage and experience of an EV from being a truly seamless one.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The call, therefore, to ensure the prominence, locatability and the predictability of availability of charging stations is a crucial one, and the placement and rollout of charging points must be one that takes into account the travel patterns of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Further, it is critical that, as a country, we start off on the right note on setting the norms of the sharing culture of charging points.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Until the day when charging points are truly ubiquitous, it would be a situation where there are more EVs needing to be charged than charging points available and there will, certainly, be a transitional period needed while the dust settles on sharing norms.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Should the norm be one where it is first-come-first-served?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Or should there be weighted preferential arrangement for vehicles that are used for livelihoods or saving lives?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Perhaps, there could be special decals for certain vehicles.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Perhaps, it is setting aside charging points to be used only by certain vehicles within key timeframes.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Perhaps, it is allowing corporations the liberty of putting in their own charging points for their employees, partners and members.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What is clear though is that there needs to be awareness, education and even public campaigns on the considerations of various driver communities and our suggested sharing norms.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is the same in the EV ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: EVs are still more expensive to procure than ICE vehicles, and though they promise lower running costs, the nascency of the EV ecosystem still incurs drivers some costs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For example, a concern for private hire and taxi drivers is the cost surrounding the prolonged usage of car parks while charging their vehicles in these car parks mandated to provide EV charging.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The concerns I have outlined here, notwithstanding, I would like to share with the House that there are, indeed, good tailwinds for the adoption of EV amongst our P2P community.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I recall that some time last year, I was a happy witness to Mr Ah Ban, one of our taxi leaders picking up his new EV car.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We marvelled about the quietness of the electric car and the technology behind it.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We appreciated happily the savings made from moving from petrol to electricity, and we were positive about the changes EVs would make to our lives.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And, indeed, Mr Ah Ban, adapted very quickly to the changes he needed to make as an EV driver.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I was very glad to hear that during those times, besides taking a meal or a drink to replenish himself, he also uses this time to go to the gym for a quick run, as the charging point he frequents has a nearby gym with shower facilities.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The move to EV for Mr Ah Ban was an awesome move, not just only for sustainability or his driving trade, but also for his mental and physical well-being.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Minister Iswaran stated in a June 2022 The Straits Times article that electric cars accounted for 8.4% of all new car registrations in the first five months of this year, more than twice the rate in all of 2021.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Compared to the whole of 2020, just two years ago, the 8.4% represents a 20-fold jump.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To support our ambition of being environmentally responsible in lowering emissions from our land transport, we must create an efficient, economical and effective EV charging ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, I have a few clarifications to make for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Bill will require all chargers in Singapore to be installed, certified and used in accordance with prescribed standards, such as registering before they can be used.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Registered chargers will need to be inspected regularly in accordance with the relevant standards.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, I would like to make a few clarifications.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What are the frequency and cost of this routine inspection?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Understandably, LTA is responsible for EV chargers in public spaces.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But is LTA also responsible for overseeing the upkeep of EV chargers in condominiums, residences and private offices?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Will LTA be adequately resourced in terms of both personnel and capability to carry out such an activity?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This involves having personnel with the necessary technical expertise to monitor and manage the supply and modification of EV chargers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With 60,000 public chargers across the country, not including chargers in office buildings, condominiums, landed homes, what is the expected manpower requirement and how do we ensure LTA is sufficiently resourced to carry out this enforcement?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Is the Ministry concerned that the Electric Vehicle Charging Operators (EVCOs) may detrimentally affect the grid and that adequate safeguards are in place to prevent that from happening?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Is LTA best equipped to comprehend and monitor its effects, or should EMA also be involved, too?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Bill requires EV charging operators to obtain a licence in order to provide the service.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Licensees will be required to meet conditions, such as data exchange, the purchase of public liability insurance and the uptime of their chargers in their network.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Licences will be valid for a fixed period and must be renewed.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, I would like to raise a few clarifications.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What kind of information must the EVCOs share?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can we ensure the user's privacy is protected?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How is the service uptime determined and what is the expected penalty for not meeting service uptime?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With multiple charging firms now offering varied pricing models, how do we ensure that the price structure is fair for customers, particularly penalty charges for leaving a fully-charged EV in an EV lot?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Thirdly, the Bill will mandate developers of specified building works to provide EV charging at their developments.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we maximise the efficiency of the charging infrastructure network?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At present, we have SP Group, Shell Recharge, BlueCharge, Charge+, CDG Engie, Plugshare, all with their own standards, apps, locations and charging speeds.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the long term, as more EVs become available, demand for ICE vehicles will also fall, as will demand for pumps at gas stations.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What is the strategy for gradually repurposing land for petrol stations and the labour that backs it up?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we ensure that the transition from ICE to EVs is done in a manageable way, for both labour and land?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One other topic that I would like to touch on is the recycling of batteries.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How are we prepared for scrapping, particularly the recycling of lithium-ion batteries in hybrid and electric vehicles?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In Singapore, what percentage of scrapped electric or hybrid vehicles had their batteries removed and recycled?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Is the Government working on regulations to ensure that hybrid and electric vehicles are recycled efficiently?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We aspire to save the environment and reduce carbon emissions from our vehicles.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Singapore must develop a resilient and effective EV charging ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: First, will LTA be responsible for chargers in private locations, such as condominiums and office buildings?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What is the possibility of EVCOs affecting the electric grid and how can we prevent that from happening?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Second, to ensure satisfactory service, what penalties will be imposed on users who park their cars in the charging lot for too long?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can we ensure that the charging pricing structure is fair and affordable for consumers?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Considering that the demand for petrol station pumps will decline as Singapore switches to electric vehicles, what are the plans to help petrol station workers transition to other sectors?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): Notwithstanding the points of clarification, Mr Speaker, Sir, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, I would like to speak about this Bill's impact on employees in vehicle repair and maintenance companies.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With the expansion of the EV charging network, consumers may now be more inclined to purchase an EV as it poses greater convenience to them and contributes better to Singapore's Green Plan 2030.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What would then be the indirect impact on employees in vehicle maintenance and repair companies and how will the Government ensure that the employees do not lose their job because their skills are now deemed less relevant and if the workforce does not have the skills required as the auto industry shifts to electric vehicles and digital services?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the USA, for instance, earlier this year in August, Ford terminated 3,000 staff, both permanent and contract, in mostly North America and India.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This was part of their restructuring efforts to better compete in the race to develop EVs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Reason for termination was due to employees' lack of skills to shift to EVs and digital services in car manufacturing.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In general, EVs have lesser parts than an ICE vehicle.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While Singapore does not manufacture ICE vehicles, we do have a considerable number of ICE vehicle repair and maintenance workshops.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The amount of repair and maintenance works is directly proportional to the amount of manufactured parts in a vehicle.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While MOT and LTA propose keeping compliance costs reasonable, has there been an estimated range for this?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would it be a one-time payment, for instance, a monthly instalment, or are there any renewable fees?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Under the licensing requirements, EVCOs are subjected to the following set of requirements, such as data sharing, third party liability insurance, payment methods, cybersecurity protections and service downtime recovery.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In this situation, what if EVCOs are unable to afford to ensure the relevant cybersecurity protection and liability insurance?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the future, when there are newer types of technology in EV chargers, would EVCOs need to go through the entire licensing process again and what if the costs associated with that are prohibitive?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Lastly, this Bill states the need for two competent persons to certify a charger unit for both deployment and regular checks.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Will the Ministry provide guidance on the endorsement cost which competent persons should charge, or will the Ministry leave this to market pricing?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Moving on to the second part of my speech, where I seek to clarify a few technical points in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Clause 25 imposes an obligation on the registered responsible person for an EV charger to cause EV chargers to be inspected by a prescribed competent person in accordance with the prescribed frequency and standards.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Within domestic premises, such as landed property, with fixed charging stations, the registered responsible persons are subjected to these periodic inspections.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How then will LTA ensure that the competent persons have the authority to enter the private premises?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, SP officers have previously faced challenges in conducting checks of these private estates' power meters when these were installed inside the home.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Clause 24 deals with unlawful installation of fixed EV chargers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, as the Bill is vague on how the Ministry would determine if one is a charger equipment specialist, it will be useful if there is a framework in identifying this competent person.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The eligibility criteria can take reference from the LEW skills structure to be considered as an industry specialist/competent person.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Second, will LTA look into having a skills transformation roadmap to allow for upskilling of workers to be a charger equipment specialist?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, is LTA working with CET institutions to create curriculums to ensure that sufficient training capacity dovetails with the demand for training of charger equipment specialists?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How many competent persons can LTA produce in the following five years and beyond?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Do we anticipate enough talent in Singapore to increase the volume of competent persons required by the market?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Training centres may not be able to cope with the sudden influx of demand for training.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
