text: Regulators will need to take into account the lead time required as we do not want a situation where providers are not able to enter the market because they were not able to complete the relevant training by the deadline.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These are similar points made the hon Members, Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Mr Ang Wei Neng, earlier.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The availability of sufficient charger equipment specialists is essential for the timely deployment of EV chargers and ensure market price for endorsements remains competitive.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This can also address potential job losses in the ICE vehicle repair and maintenance industry.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Third, as it is common for hardware manufacturers to enforce the need to engage their staff or approved maintenance contractors for repairs and servicing, does LTA anticipate such market practices imposed by EV charger manufacturers?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If so, would independent charger equipment specialists be able to certify a charger is fit for use?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This would have implications for the cost levied on EVCOs and end users.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Lastly, can the same competent person perform the role of LEW and charger equipment specialist?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, would there be any reconciliation between the EV Charging Bill and CPFTA?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would EV chargers be added to this list, be parked under the CPFTA's safety mark?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Since there is already an existing safety regulation under controlled goods, parking EV chargers under the same regulation would prevent double certification and duplication of man-hour efforts by regulators.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I wish to also highlight the Management Corporation Strata Title (MCST)-related Act amendments and the questions and concerns raised by these stakeholders when I interacted with them.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, there are some challenges that can result in social issues, the first of which is the issue of idling.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Residents may become unhappy with MCSTs and Town Councils and neighbourly disputes may occur.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Second, MCSTs have shared that, despite the amendments to the Building Maintenance and Strata Management Act where the threshold for MCSTs will be a simple majority of votes, there are still challenges.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: When the demand for EVs goes up, who will bear the expansion and upgrading cost of substations for higher power provisions?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As condominiums are considered private housing, there are no Government grants to co-fund power upgrades for chargers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some condominiums do not have sufficient power supply to allocate for EV chargers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As there are now market-based solutions where EVCOs lease lots from MCSTs to install chargers and recover investments from the revenue of usage, is this grant still relevant?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would providing grants for MCSTs to co-fund power upgrades be considered instead?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, the impact on relevant stakeholders, such as vehicle repair and maintenance companies, EVCOs and residents; second, the relevant concerns in specific clauses of the Bill; and lastly, questions raised by MCSTs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Notwithstanding my clarifications and suggestions, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Introducing and expanding a new infrastructure is always a significant undertaking.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But laying a strong foundation early promotes certainty and stability among stakeholders and users.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It will help our drivers to use cleaner energy and meet Singapore's sustainability targets in the long run.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I have suggestions and clarifications in four areas.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Speaker, Sir, are the proposed minimum number of charging points adequate?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As such, we need to beef up the number of charging points across the island.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, the Bill proposes a relatively small number of all parking spaces in the development to have charging points.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Would this conservative number of mandated available charging points move the needle?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Would this encourage higher EV adoption in the near future?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can we not afford to have more ambitious targets?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I understand that there is an ongoing study to determine what will encourage Singaporeans to adopt EVs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The results are slated to be released in the second quarter of 2023.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How does this translate to the ratio of charging spaces to the number of EVs?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We should establish a national EV adoption or conversion rate target.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This would better guide us to determine the adequacy of charging points.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, while the spotlight has been on personal cars, electric forms of commercial vehicles are also becoming popular, like lorries and buses.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: An example is a new ride-sharing service next year that allows SMEs to rent electric vans at 20 locations across Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: All this is good news for our sustainability targets and should be encouraged.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are these new developments and increased demands for EV charging factored into our targets?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mr Speaker, Sir, human behavioural issues could undermine the actual availability of charging points.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I am aware of complaints about EVs hogging charging points when they are fully charged or not charging.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Likewise, there are non-EVs that misuse the parking lots designated for EVs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: LTA explained that EVs, generally, only have to be charged once every five to seven days.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This was one of the factors taken into account for setting the target quota.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Even so, it would be idealistic to assume that users would, by default, seek out consensus or compromise on a schedule to use the charging points on different days.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Moreover, does the target number of charging points take into consideration the prevalence of private hire vehicles and the high mileage that would be clocked by private hire vehicles?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As we work on expanding the infrastructure, can we look into enforcing appropriate parking?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are there deterrent measures or penalties for drivers who park erroneously in lots reserved for EVs?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This brings to mind the fines imposed on those who park at designated disabled parking lots.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can we do more to formalise codes of conduct to encourage considerate behaviour for EV charging?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Legislation will also not be enough in this case.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Speaker, Sir, what are the plans to mandate EV charging at existing developments with no upgrading plans?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To promote nation-wide adoption, our EV infrastructure must be comprehensive.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Ministry clarify what is the projected percentage of buildings in Singapore that would have to comply with mandated provision of EV chargers?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With the ongoing high interest rate environment, there is the likelihood that many developments have suspended plans for upgrading works.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As such, how effective will the requirements to increase EV charging facilities be during this period, where plans to upgrade are likely to be suspended?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, many people go to work in such buildings.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Instead of charging their vehicles at work, they would have to compete with their neighbours back home for the limited charging lots.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Worse still, they may leave their cars to charge in the residential car park and hog the lot while at work.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will the Government monitor the installation rate of EV charging points in strata-titled developments?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For developments that consistently refuse to install EV charging points, will efforts be made to engage them and address their concerns?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We are looking at the potential exclusion of a significant number of drivers if strata-titled residential buildings deny their residents of EV charging lots.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Concomitantly, I would like to ask the Government to consider providing additional support or subsidies for brownfield sites.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Out of this list, slightly fewer than 10 are major players.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The rest are smaller providers, with some providing EV charging as a side business.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we ensure that among providers, there is healthy competition?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On the other hand, how do we avoid the problem of having too many small players and the risk of a fragmented market?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We have already seen a similar scenario in our energy market.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We are just coming out of a pandemic.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With the Ukrainian war and geopolitical uncertainties causing inflationary pressures as well as disruptions in energy supplies, there is a risk that nations focus on the pressing issues of the day but lose sight of the climate and energy crisis facing the planet.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must take the long-term view, focus on the clean energy transition and give due attention to the existential crisis of our generation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must be bold and ambitious with our targets to evoke significant changes in attitudes towards transportation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Singapore must always be one-step ahead with our planning to meet future needs and demands in the EV landscape.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As part of the Steward Pillar in our Forward Singapore conversations, we must also continue to engage our residents on how Singapore can do better in environmental sustainability, as well as grow our partnerships for a green, liveable and climate-resilient Singapore.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.35 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.15 pm until 3.35 pm.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With the increasing number of EVs on our roads, it is necessary for us to legislate the charging of EVs to ensure safety and accessibility of reliable chargers all over our island.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I have a clarification for MOT – will these chargers be allowed to continue usage beyond these six months?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Speaker, Sir, in Mandarin, please (In Mandarin):   My next question is regarding power capacity.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What are the Government’s plans to ensure that public carparks, industrial parks, public and private buildings, bus terminals, hospitals, amongst others, will have enough and the required electric power capacities?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition, what safety preparations and back-up measures do we have in the event of flooding of areas with these chargers?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English): I would like to urge for incentives for private apartments and condominiums to install chargers so that potential owners will have less range anxiety and switch to EVs with confidence.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In line with the Singapore Green Plan 2030 to promote EV adoption, Singaporeans can tap on many business and job opportunities.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I urge LTA to collaborate with the private sector players like the banks.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, UOB has put in place financing to promote the development of the EV sector and the transition to green vehicles.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will the Government consider extending the scheme to encourage more owners to switch to EVs?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Alternatively, would MOT consider a separate COE category for EVs, considering the past few years’ take-up rate for EVs to determine the EV COE quota size?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On the COEs for EVs, can LTA consider extending the COE life from the current 10 years to a longer period, say 12 years, at the same quota premium?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will be another incentive to encourage owners to switch to EVs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The PARF rebate, if any, which is at 50% of ARF at the end of 10 years, should be reduced, in tandem, to 45% and 40% at end of the 11th and 12th year respectively.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the Government consider allowing some rebates or incentives at point of purchase and/or for the usage of EVs manufactured in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, waivers of ERP and road tax and free parking at public car parks for a period of time may be attractive to potential EV buyers.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I also urge MOT to consider more incentives for private apartments and condominiums to install chargers so that potential owners will have less range anxiety and switch to EVs with confidence.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We also need a clear framework to minimise inappropriate use and hogging of charging lots and ensure that EVs can have access to chargers easily.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There are more companies awarded tenders to install public chargers these days.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Each service provider decides on its chargers and uses its own app to facilitate payment and the chargers’ locations.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will the Government consider developing a single app to integrate all service providers and set a common charging rate across all?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, I am concerned about the issues of batteries, as in the utilisation of batteries, swapping services and recycling.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I understand that batteries are resource-intensive, requiring up to two batteries for a vehicle on the road.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What is the Ministry’s view on this and should we be more mindful about not encouraging battery-swapping schemes?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Old batteries may generate a lot of toxic chemicals and potentially cause explosions.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The recycling and disposal of such batteries is still an industry in its nascent stage.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As EVs are adopted by the rest of South-east Asia, Singapore can, potentially, become a regional centre for battery recycling and disposal.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If we can close the loop by taking care of EVs from purchasing to charging and maintenance and, finally, to disposal, we will be able to transit smoothly into the adoption and development of this sector.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It enables Singapore to scale up the provision of EV charging in a reliable, accelerated way.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first clarification is on clause 97, which amends the Building Maintenance and Strata Management Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is welcome news for many condominium owners, whose management has been unable to install charging points because a small minority of the residents object.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is also welcome news for Singapore’s Green Plan.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: More charging points at home mean more drivers making the leap from gas cars to electric cars.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It will help us reach our net-zero emissions target.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But I am concerned that the lowered voting threshold is limited.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It applies only when the motion does not propose spending from the MCST’s management or sinking fund.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister explain the intent for this carve-out?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The management and sinking funds of MCSTs are meant precisely for the installation and maintenance of common property, such as charging points.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Is the idea for operators of charging points to bear all costs and for residents to pay the operator out of pocket?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is not how charging points are funded at most condos around the world, so, any clarification on intent and implementation will be helpful.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second clarification is on Part 8, which mandates the installation of charging points during major construction works.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The amendment fails to cover redevelopments where the gross floor area, or GFA, increases by less than 50%.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share how many building projects from 2018 to 2020 increased the GFA by between 25% and 50%, and how many increased the GFA by between 10% and 25%?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The amendment also fails to cover redevelopments where the new approved electrical-load capacity is less than 280 kilovolt-ampere.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share how many building projects from 2018 to 2020 led to a new approved electrical load of between 150 and 280 kilovolt-ampere?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I worry that we have set reasonable standards but applied them to too few building projects.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Indeed, it would be unsurprising if redevelopments in the coming years are designed to dodge our threshold for the charging point standards.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My suggestion is that we should impose standards even on smaller-scale redevelopments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These standards may be lower, but they must exist.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That will ensure a more steady growth in our charging-point provisions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third and final clarification is not about what is in the Bill but what is missing from it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Several key ingredients for increasing the provision of charging points are not in the Bill today.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Government share how many charging points have been supported by the co-funding from the EV Common Charger Grant?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Are we on track to co-fund the grant maximum of 2,000 charging points by end-2023?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If the grant remains underutilised, then there might be scope to increase the quantum of the grant or to expand the number of co-funded charging points per residence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Does the Ministry plan to install charging points on the kerbs of residential streets and public roads?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Street parking is the norm for many Singaporeans in both residential and commercial areas.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For some, it is the only place they can park.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should ensure there are options for kerbside charging as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the US city of Seattle, the city government is installing kerbside charging points free of charge if the applicant's home does not have its own parking facilities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should have our own programme, based on a framework that balances costs, accessibility and any other considerations.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: They have raised a series of questions and suggestions on a range of issues pertaining to the Bill and I will endeavour to address them.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In particular, my responses will focus on the broad policy points pertaining to safety, reliability and accessibility, which are the key thrusts of this legislation.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: First, on the issue of safety-related regulations, which will apply to all chargers, including those which are already installed.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked whether it is excessive to have three separate regimes for approval, registration and licensing.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The registration regime holds each charger owner accountable for the safe use and maintenance of their chargers.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The licensing regime ensures the reliability of EV charging services.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, there are distinct objectives served by these various components.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Together, these regimes minimise the harm from unsafe charging, as Assoc Prof Jamus Lim has highlighted.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That includes the examples that Mr Saktiandi raised, where even if there may be instances where two separate approvals are required, where they coincide with the applicant because it is one and the same, we will endeavour to streamline those processes to minimise friction.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Edward Chia asked if the proposed regulatory regime should be reconciled with or parked under the regulatory regime for Controlled Goods in the Consumer Protection (Safety Requirements) Regulations.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: However, those regulations are targeted at the description and advertisement of goods.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As I have explained earlier, the scope of this Bill goes further and a dedicated regulatory regime under LTA is what we have assessed to be the preferred and more appropriate option.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Saktiandi, Mr Sharael Taha and Mr Shawn Huang have also asked for more details of the homologation, certification and inspection regimes.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: These technical standards were just revised earlier this year, in consultation with industry experts and academics.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, Members can be assured that the EV charging industry is familiar with the standards as the industry has played an active role in its review.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: LTA will continue to work closely with the industry on regular future reviews as well.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: LTA is also working with industry players to support local R&D on promising EV charging technologies while ensuring safety, such as through regulatory sandboxes.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Saktiandi asked if we have any insights into the charging solutions for motorcycles.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The sandboxes for motorcycle charging are in the very early stages.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It would be premature for us to infer at this stage.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But we do expect to learn quite a bit from these and other sandboxes so that we can, eventually, generalise the application through appropriate regulation.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: On Mr Gan Thiam Poh's question, we take fire safety very seriously.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Under the revised Fire Code, EV chargers must have an isolation switch to cut off the electricity supply to the EV charger to facilitate emergency response.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is in addition to other charger design requirements in the TR25, such as electrical circuit breakers that minimise the risk of electrocution and electrical fires, including in the event of flooding mentioned by Mr Don Wee.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But, in general, many Members have highlighted this concern about fires.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And this is one of the reasons why we have paid specific attention to this and worked closely with SCDF.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: On Mr Dennis Tan's query, we are planning for the charging demand of a largely electric light vehicle population, taking into account the average mileage of car drivers in Singapore and the effective range of a typical EV.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: There are different parameters and these are factored into the computation.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But having said that, I want to emphasise that we are dealing with an evolving space.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The technology is evolving, the adoption rates and, therefore, the consequential demand are also changing.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Usage patterns, both in terms of driving and charging habits, have yet to normalise.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, we need time to monitor and assess this pattern.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It allows us to deploy quickly but without incurring some of the heavier capital expenditures (capex) – the capex that is associated with, for example, the upgrading of substations.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Instead, we are able to roll out the charging infrastructure in this first phase quickly because it focuses on the more approximate or last-mile type of infrastructure, such as the distribution boxes and so on, and then, of course, the actual charging points themselves.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We want to deploy charging infrastructure quickly to support EV adoption.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The data we gather from this adoption will inform how we want to go further.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We may not need to wait until 2025 because, if the data comes in earlier and the patterns become more discernible, then we will have to adjust accordingly.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As Mr Ang Wei Neng said, we also need to avoid overprovisioning, especially as the EV population today is relatively small, although the take-up rates are rising.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, in LTA's recent large-scale tender for charging points at HDB car parks, operators start with deploying at least three charging points at each car park, with the flexibility to scale up to 12 charging points.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: LTA will monitor the demand and launch further tenders as necessary.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, essentially, we can ramp up supply, if the need arises.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We expect the vast majority of charging points to be low-powered.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This optimises the electrical capacity required as charging can be done overnight when there is less demand on grid capacity.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: However, as Assoc Prof Jamus Lim and Ms Yeo Wan Ling have said, some EV users will require fast charging, such as two-shift taxi drivers.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng was concerned about the ground issues in implementation.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is a legitimate concern because when we take it to the ground, to the individual HDB car parks, there may be no end of questions around which floor of the car park the EV charging point should be deployed.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: On this, we have LTA and HDB, among other important agencies that have relevant jurisdiction, in order to make sure that we are able to iron out these sorts of teething issues on the ground as we implement because we do not want these kinds of, if you like, regulatory hurdles to get in the way of a quick deployment of the chargers that we wish to achieve.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As Mr Sharael Taha has highlighted, the role of petrol stations will also have to evolve as EVs become more widespread.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Some petrol stations have already started to provide fast chargers for EVs and many electric taxi drivers charge there.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The licensing regime is essential to our plans as it allows LTA to set conditions, such as service uptime, and also to collect data on EV charging patterns.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Such data is critical to support the national master-planning efforts to deploy chargers and upgrade electrical infrastructure.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: However, accessibility goes beyond the physical infrastructure and it includes user experience.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is where Mr Don Wee's suggestion about developing a single app to integrate all service providers is pertinent.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is, indeed, what LTA has been working on.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Today, LTA's MyTransport App allows EV users to locate and access public charging points offered by various EVCOs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: LTA has just launched a beta function displaying real-time charger availability on the app, which more operators will contribute to over time.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: LTA is also working with third-party platform providers to allow more EV users to access charger information on their platform of choice, including information on real-time availability.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I want to assure Mr Sharael Taha and, indeed, all Members that LTA will be transparent about how licensees' data is used.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Commercially sensitive data will only be used for LTA's internal master-planning work.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In general, LTA will not require EVCOs to share any personal data and LTA will only use or disclose any data collected from licensees in compliance with directions made under the Public Sector (Governance) Act and other relevant laws relating to confidentiality.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng, Ms Yeo Wan Ling and Mr Edward Chia asked about preventing and deterring the inappropriate use of EV charging lots.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Today, in HDB car parks, it is already an offence for a non-EV to park in an EV charging lot.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: EVCOs are also commercially driven to tackle this, because if a car is occupying the lot but not charging, that is loss of revenue.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In some countries, EVCOs have implemented idle fees and time-based pricing to discourage lot hogging.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Others are looking into technological solutions to make enforcement easier.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Enforcement aside, motorists must also develop a culture of responsible and gracious behaviour when charging their EVs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, education and an evolving culture are key.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The fact is, even with enforcement and education, it will take some time for the EV charging behaviour and patterns in Singapore to normalise.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We need a collective effort to help nurture the process and allow us all to ensure that this experience is a positive one for all of us.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Several Members have posed more detailed questions about the licensing regime.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Thirdly, let me elaborate on the mandate to provide EV charging at certain developments.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Saktiandi has asked why developments owned by the Government are not subject to this statutory requirement.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As with other provisions like parking, Government-owned developments will take reference from our general policy and abide by relevant internal circulars.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We have already started, as Members know, to deploy EV chargers on a large scale at HDB residential estates.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I also have it on good authority – from Mr Speaker no less – that Parliament is also looking into the installation of EV chargers in the car park here.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, Members can all model responsible EV charging behaviour and the recalcitrant ones will, I think, face consequences in the Chamber.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We will monitor EV adoption trends and consider whether the mandate should be extended to all developments in future.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The Bill does allow the Minister for Transport to adjust these thresholds through regulations when needed.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In the meantime, we encourage developers to plan ahead and invest in the requisite infrastructure.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Louis Ng, in particular, was concerned that the lowered voting threshold for strata-titled developments only applies to proposals that do not tap on MCST funds.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The reason for this is simple – it is to preserve a certain equivalence in the current level of accountability and governance for the use of MCST funds.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Even then, we expect the lower threshold to be able to facilitate the installation of EV charging points because it is not a very capital-intensive exercise, based on the way it is being carried out today.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The more prevalent practice is for EVCOs to pay for the cost of installation upfront and recover it from EV users over time.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, part of the challenge here is helping the condominium MCSTs navigate the process because they may not know how to go about it and so on.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, LTA and BCA will work with industry players to develop guides to help condominium residents in the process of installing EV chargers.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Several Members have asked about the enforcement of the Bill.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: LTA will take a pragmatic approach, with safety as the paramount objective.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As all chargers must be registered before use, the records of the Registered Responsible Person for each charger will facilitate enforcement efforts.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Specifically, on Mr Edward Chia's question, clause 74 of the Bill allows an authorised officer to enter premises where that officer believes, on reasonable grounds, that specific safety-related offences are being committed.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Don Wee asked about the transitional arrangements for existing chargers.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is to protect the public from potentially unsafe chargers.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In this intervening period, until the Act commences, both on the supply side, suppliers will now take reference from this and will have to ensure that the models they are selling are homologated or belong to the homologated variety.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: For if they fail, then customers will be back with them within six months to see what can be done to remedy it.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And I would urge all who are contemplating procuring the chargers to also take reference from this requirement.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: First, on the long-term market structure of the EV charging industry.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I agree with Mr Gan Thiam Poh and Mr Yip Hon Weng that it is crucial to ensure healthy competition among EVCOs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Thus far, we have seen healthy competition in the EV charging industry, supported by the growth in market entrants over the past two years.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng, Mr Sharael Taha and Mr Saktiandi Supaat have asked how the Government will ensure that EV charging services are priced fairly.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Fundamentally, competition and consumer choice are the most effective means of doing so.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But we will monitor the price dispersion – something that Mr Ang Wei Neng raised.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I understand that, today, the price dispersion across different charging is about five cents per kilowatt-hour.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But I would like to point out that there is an inherent irony in this because, if there is a wide dispersion in the prices, does that mean that we have a more competitive market?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And if we have a very narrow dispersion or, in extremis, just a single price across the whole of Singapore, is that a desirable outcome?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, we have to think about this carefully.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But, in the first instance, our objective has been to ensure that the award of the tenders and so on is to address the key point that Mr Ang Wei Neng has been raising, which is really not having too wide a dispersion.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The other thing to bear in mind is – not unlike what we see with the conventional ICE cars and so on – I am very sure that the EVCOs will provide incentives and other benefits to their regular customers.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, that would be a further discount, if you will, on the prices being paid.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, we need to really look at this in great detail and understand the true impact before we make any further judgements on the matter.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Second, Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Mr Ang Wei Neng asked about manpower development to support the EV transition.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Nevertheless, EMA has been reaching out to Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) to raise awareness of the prerequisites to become an LEW.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: EMA has also implemented alternate pathways to allow experienced workers to apply for LEW licences.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As for charging equipment specialists, to respond to Mr Edward Chia, EVCOs have been building up their talent pool and already employ such specialists in-house.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: LTA is working with the industry to provide clarity on the requirements to be a charging equipment specialist under this regulatory regime.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As Mr Edward Chia has also highlighted, our technicians and mechanics will also need to be equipped to take on the opportunities offered by the EV industry.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Automotive technicians who have undergone relevant training on high voltage systems safety awareness can be certified under this scheme.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We will continue to work closely with the industry and IHLs to grow our talent pool.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Thirdly, I agree with Mr Sharael Taha and Mr Don Wee that we must ensure the proper disposal and recycling of EV batteries.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, everyone in the ecosystem will have to comply with it.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I have only been at MOT about a year, but no conversation on the vehicle system is complete without a discussion on COEs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, I thank them for bringing it up.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The core objective of the COE system is to limit our vehicle population.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We have set the vehicle population growth to be zero and to have an efficient mechanism to allocate the quota.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is the case for all vehicles and an EV is a vehicle.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is not also good policy to foist too many objectives on a single policy tool.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, I would argue, for Members' consideration, that to use the COE for multiple objectives is not an appropriate or suitable policy formulation.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: One of the proposals that Members have made – and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim in particular, I think – is to have a new segment for EVs, if I heard him correctly.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: If we think through the implications of that proposal, what it means is that we will have to take away supply from the other categories in order to supply a new category called EVs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The total supply for the different segments will reduce further.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And for EVs, you will have a specific category.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, I am assuming, in the Member's policy design proposal, EV buyers can only buy EV COEs and not any other COE.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And if you think through that, you are going to have far more, minimally, volatility in the price because the supply is constrained and, potentially, higher prices.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It also raises a bunch of questions around how you make that allocative decision – on what basis?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And what is the argument that substantiates that allocative decision?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: What we do is we treat all vehicles the same because the COE system is designed to control vehicle population, full stop.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Whether you are ICE, hybrid, electric, maybe, in future, fuel cell hydrogen, they are all vehicles on our roads.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And then, what we do is we directly incentivise the adoption of the kinds of vehicles that we would like to promote through other policy tools for intervention.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: There was a suggestion that maybe we can give a 10% discount.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Even at today’s COE prices, $45,000 is significantly higher than that in terms of upfront cost.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: There was another point raised – and I wanted to just make sure and that is why I sought the clarification from the Member Assoc Prof Jamus Lim – because the initial point in his speech was that PHC drivers are concerned because the cost of EVs is 82% higher.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I think he said, in fact, operating cost.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And when I asked for clarification, he said, no, it is actually ownership cost.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, I had a cursory look at the site that he was using – paultan.org, I understand, is the site.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In fact, the quote goes further than just 82% higher ownership costs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It actually says 82% higher ownership costs in the region, not just in Singapore.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, it is not very clear where the number comes from and, in particular, whether it has taken into account all the schemes that we have in the context of Singapore.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The point I want to make is this.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: When you consider costs, there are different elements to these.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: There is the upfront ownership cost, which seems to take into account the specific schemes that we have put in place; there is the operating cost for the life cycle – and on that, I can assure you that, in fact, EVs are very competitive.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Because simply on the basis of cost per kilometre, based on today’s prices, it is at least no more than half what it would cost if you were driving an ICE.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I am not promoting EVs – or I am not selling them – but these are the facts.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And it does not take into account the maintenance costs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Because an EV has about 20 moving parts, compared to an ICE vehicle which has got, I am told by engineers, 2,000 moving parts.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, when you total it all up, actually, the equation balances out.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Perhaps, what is required is for greater information and awareness amongst those who are making the choices, including PHC drivers, so that they have the full picture.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But I thought it was important to make this clarification because we do not want us to be citing Internet sources but without seeing them through in terms of the specific application in our context.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: To Mr Dennis Tan’s question, the electrification of goods vehicles is, in fact, one of our priorities.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In fact, the light goods vehicles segment saw the highest rate of EV adoption this year, at around 28%.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The part that is more challenging is the very heavy vehicles, the big trucks and so on.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And the reason is because, from the point of view of propulsion power and so on, there are trade-offs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is why I mentioned in my earlier speech that hydrogen or related fuel types are being considered quite actively in that regard.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I have endeavoured to address all their queries in the main and I would like to assure Members that MOT and LTA will study and, where possible, incorporate their suggestions in the design and implementation of the EV charging system.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Our vision is to have a vehicle population that is electric.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But that will require the collective effort of Government, industry, unions and consumers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: First, I absolutely have no difficulty with the notion that the COE should be kept predominantly for focusing on the overall body of vehicles.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But that said, if I understand correctly, if LTA will, indeed, stop issuing COEs for ICE vehicles after 2030, would not this, ultimately, be equivalent to issuing a specialised category of EV COEs which will apply to all cars after 2030 and then, you will have an existing stock of COEs for cars from before?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The second point is, I would like to acknowledge that the Minister is correct.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I misspoke when I said it was the operating cost.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Indeed, it is the full ownership cost that I should have cited.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: That said, the figure was, as I clarified earlier on, a statement from a Vice President at Grab, which is a local outfit and it was in the context of the Eco Prosperity Conference in June this year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I believe Minister Iswaran was one of the keynote speakers at that conference.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, I do believe that this 82% – again, it is not my estimate, but her estimate – was said in the local context.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I may have been at the conference, but I cannot take accountability for what was said there by other speakers.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But I am just pulling out what was on the website and it says the total cost of owning an EV remains 82% higher than owning an equivalent ICE, four-wheeled vehicle – and then, it said, “in the region, Ms Goh said”.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, I think it is an important point of detail, does the Member not think so?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Because the region has got significant variations and, certainly, what it means is that the number that has been cited here does not necessarily take into — I do not know whether it did, but it would appear, at first reading, that it has not taken that into account.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We already have to deal with a lot of misinformation outside.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, at least in the Chamber, when we cite sources and so on, let us just make sure we get the facts right.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That was my main objective: to make sure that we got it right, so that whether it is a PHC driver or an HDB family wanting to buy a car or anyone else, they have the full information and the right information so that they can make the appropriate choice that fits their circumstances.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But they are all treated the same, they are in the same bucket and we treat it that way.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We are not allocating a specific amount for electric, we are not allocating a specific amount for hybrid and so on.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We are just taking it as one policy position.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: What the Member is proposing is, actually, to deconstruct the current COE allocation and quota, and create new elements.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: My point is that this is something I do not think we need to have a PhD in Economics to infer this.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That might actually end up frustrating the very objective of the Member's proposal.      .
